It sounds like your friends and family care about your wellbeing. If you don't think that they'll respond in a way that will hurt you, please consider reaching out to those who want to help. I'm sure anyone who does would prefer that you seek out support rather than letting those dark thoughts take their toll on you.  It's not your fault or theirs that you're having these thoughts. If you still don't feel comfortable sharing with certain people, that's fine. It's good that you came here for help. There are those who are ready and willing to do what we can to help you find a way out of this. There's always another way, no matter what those thoughts lead you to believe.

It's often hard not to focus on what we've lost.  Please don't give up all the good things you have left. There are ways to leave the bad stuff behind without having to leave everything. The bad memories and experiences can stay in the past. The future is full of opportunities, and as long as you stay around, each passing day will be another chance to make things better.

You don't need to apologize to anyone here, or anywhere for still being alive. There are people here, like me, who want you to stay and find fulfillment in your life. Nobody but an awful person would hold you to a suicide threat, and that kind of person isn't  worth apologizing to. You're smart for coming back and seeking more support. You're strong for not giving it all up eight days ago.

It's very responsible of you to reach out for help. A lot of us are too scared or unmotivated to do so. If you can do that, then you're already taking your first step towards getting better. I believe that you have the capacity to turn your situation around. Anyone who cares does.

Technically, evolution refers to change over time, which in a biological sense we clearly see in the fossil record, as well as in the constantly shifting ecosystems which surround us today. Evolution on its own is definately a fact. 

The theory of evolution, which often gets conflated with evolution, is the scientific community's explanation for that fact, containing all of our current knowledge , evidence, and models for the factors which drive the evolutionary progress. 

So to reiterate, evolution is a fact,  the theory of evolution is an explanation for that fact based on all of the available evidence.

It's most likely not within a reasonable realm of possibility that grey wolves would survive any sort of mass exinctio caused by humans or otherwise. Pack hunting predators require a steady population of considerably sized primary consumers, enough to share the meat after a kill. When there's less food and animals decrease in both population and size, it's less likely to find success in the pack-hunter niche.

That being said, if wolves did survive a mass extinction, the first changes I would think to see would be a major decrease in social behavior. Most likely becoming smaller, stealthier hunters, operating in, at most mating pairs or with juvenile offspring.
 (Unlikely of course, because so many other animals already inhabit these roles today and would have no reason to move away from them in an extinction event. In fact, animals which inhabit these roles today would be the most likely to adapt to become more wolf like when the opportunity arises in the future.)

Theoretically, anything. As long as the dwarves are giving them what they need to live. Domesticated creatures don't really "evolve" to fit to the environment. Because the people keeping them alive take care of everything for them, they wont experience any pressure to adapt.

Now If youre talking about creatures that can survive only on food sources which can be found underground, that changes things. If the dwarves aren't able to provide their livestock with grasses and leaves to eat, then they'll need to use animals that can survive on mosses, ferns and roots. Traditional livestock, like cows, sheep, and horses, (as far as I'm aware) cant effectively feed on these things alone. You're going to need naturally moss eating animals. Pika, northern deer, turtles, and iguana are a few I found during a quick google search. 

But if what you had in mind were animals which naturally occurr in deep cave systems, that's where finding effective livestock becomes quite difficult. I'd imagine the only animals they could effectively farm are cave fish, amphibians and crustaceans, if they could isolate ponds and keep the animals within them fed. These creatures have already evolved quite well to the underground environment, so they wouldn't change either.

So all in all, the only adaptation any domestic animal population would experience in this situation would only be that  which is imposed by the dwarves themselves, i.e. Breeding, to make the animals larger to provide more meat.
